---
title: "From a questionnaire to its findings"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

A survey's quality rules live inside the form — `constraint`, `required`,
`calculate` — and they are written once, in the spreadsheet, by the person
who knows what a plausible answer looks like. The problem is that nothing in
an analysis script runs them: the data frame you read back is whatever the
devices sent, and the rules that were supposed to guard it are XML the script
never opens.

rxeval runs them. This walkthrough uses the small household form shipped with
the package, and a submission with problems planted on purpose.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(rxeval)
library(dplyr)

form       <- system.file("extdata", "visit.xml", package = "rxeval")
submission <- system.file("extdata", "visit-submission.xml", package = "rxeval")
```

## Before the field: will the form travel?

ODK forms are evaluated by two implementations — JavaRosa inside Collect and
KoboCollect, Enketo inside web forms — and neither is a superset of the
other. The gaps do not announce themselves: an expression Collect cannot
evaluate usually yields nothing rather than an error, so the form fills in,
the interview finishes, and a column comes back empty.

`form_portability()` reads the form the way both engines would:

```{r portability}
form_portability(form) |>
  as_tibble()
```

The verdict worth filtering for is `breaks`. `"both, differently"` is the
worst value it takes — nothing fails anywhere, and the two engines quietly
compute different answers. Here the form has a milder, common case: a
`calculate` built on `last()`, which Enketo evaluates and JavaRosa does not
have at all.

```{r portability-triage}
form_portability(form) |>
  filter(breaks == "Collect / KoboCollect") |>
  select(path, construct, suggestion)
```

Every issue carries a `suggestion` when there is one to give: a rewrite that
means one thing in both engines. Zero rows means the form travels.

## After the field: what do the form's own rules say?

`submission_findings()` evaluates the questionnaire's rules against collected
data and reports what does not hold:

```{r findings}
findings <- submission_findings(form, submission)

findings |>
  as_tibble()
```

Three findings, three different kinds of trouble:

```{r findings-by-kind}
findings |>
  count(kind)
```

- a **constraint** the device should have enforced and, on this submission,
  did not — 25 residents against a rule of at most 20;
- a **required** question that came back unanswered;
- a **calculation** whose stored value is not what the form computes — the
  `last()` issue found above, no longer a prediction but a hole in a column.

A rule the engine could not evaluate comes back as `kind = "not-evaluated"`,
never as a pass: a rule that did not run has not been satisfied, and
reporting it as clean would be the one failure worth avoiding.

Over a whole round, the same call is one `lapply` away:

```{r round, eval = FALSE}
list.files("submissions", full.names = TRUE) |>
  lapply(\(s) submission_findings(form, s) |> mutate(file = basename(s))) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  count(path, kind, sort = TRUE)
```

## Trying a rule by hand

`eval_expression()` answers what one expression does before it goes into the
spreadsheet — against a real submission, in the same dialect the devices
speak:

```{r eval}
eval_expression("count(/data/resident[age < 18])", submission)

eval_expression("if(/data/residents > 20, 'needs a note', 'fine')", submission)
```

An expression the engine cannot evaluate raises an error rather than
returning a plausible value — the same rule as everywhere else in rxeval:
silence is never a verdict.

## Where the rules come from

Every portability rule in the engine was decided by putting the same
expression to JavaRosa and to Enketo's evaluator and reading the two answers
— the method, and the receipts, are on the
[project site](https://milkway.github.io/rxeval/).
